lesson.title: Solubility: Finding a Solute's Breaking Point
lesson.summary: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature, a limit set by the balance between dissolving and recrystallizing rather than a hard ceiling.
lesson.body:
Solubility is the maximum quantity of a solute that will dissolve in a given quantity of solvent at a specified temperature, producing what is called a saturated solution once that limit is reached. It is usually reported as grams of solute per 100 g of solvent, or, for gases, alongside the pressure of that gas above the liquid. Solubility only makes sense as a follow up question to the last two chapters: it describes exactly how far a solvent-solute pairing can push the homogeneous mixture definition of a solution before it runs out of room.

Why is there a limit at all? Dissolving a solute means breaking some solute-solute attractions, like the ionic lattice holding a salt crystal together, and some solvent-solvent attractions, in exchange for forming new solute-solvent attractions, the same intermolecular forces covered earlier. As more and more solute dissolves, the solution eventually reaches a point where dissolved solute particles are recrystallizing back out just as fast as new solute is dissolving. That balance point, not some hard physical ceiling, is what solubility actually measures.

Temperature shifts that balance. For most solid solutes dissolving in a liquid, added thermal energy helps break apart the solute's rigid structure, so solubility tends to rise with temperature. Dissolved gases behave the opposite way: warming the solution gives gas molecules already dissolved in the liquid enough extra kinetic energy to escape back into the gas phase, so gas solubility drops as temperature rises. That is the real reason a warm soda goes flat faster than a cold one, and why warm lake water holds less dissolved oxygen, putting stress on fish and other aquatic life during heat waves.

Pressure matters too, but mainly for gas solutes: a gas dissolved in a liquid becomes more soluble as the pressure of that gas above the liquid increases, which is exactly why soda is bottled under pressure and fizzes the moment that pressure is released.

A concrete number makes the limit tangible. Sodium chloride's solubility in water is about 36 g per 100 g of water at 20°C. That means 250 g of water at that temperature can dissolve, at most, 36 g divided by 100 g, times 250 g, which works out to 90 g of NaCl. Try to add more than that and the extra solid simply will not dissolve, no matter how long you stir.
